name: TrustMRR
tagline: Connects your payment provider and issues a third-party verified MRR badge you can put on a landing page or listing.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The engineering here is trivial: read Stripe, sum active subscriptions, render an SVG. The product is not the SVG, it is the fact that someone other than you did the arithmetic. A badge you generated yourself, hosted on your own domain, reading from your own API key, is a number you typed in a nicer font. Buyers, acquirers and directory readers discount self-attested revenue to roughly zero, and rightly so. You can absolutely build the dashboard for yourself, you just cannot build the credibility.
coreLoopDIY: Pulls active subscriptions from your Stripe account, computes normalized MRR, and serves a cached SVG badge plus a small public stats page.
requirements: Stripe account with a restricted read-only API key
Somewhere to host a tiny always-on Node service
A domain or subdomain if you want the badge to look like it belongs to you
whatYouLose: Third-party attestation, which is the entire point
Tamper resistance: nothing stops you from hardcoding the number, and everyone knows it
Any discovery or directory effect from being listed alongside other verified products
Support for providers you have not written adapters for: Paddle, Lemon Squeezy, RevenueCat, App Store
Someone else's uptime, so a dead badge on your landing page is now your problem
moatNotes: Verification products live or die on whether the reader recognizes the verifier. That recognition is bought with years and other people's listings, not code.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the buyer of a verified MRR badge is not buying software, they are renting someone else's reputation for one line on a sales page. Indie makers listing on acquisition marketplaces, pitching investors, or running a "we hit 10k MRR" launch need a number a stranger will believe, and the only way to get that is to hand read-only access to a neutral party who has already convinced everyone else to trust it. The self-hosted version is genuinely useful as a private revenue dashboard, and completely useless for the job the product is hired to do.
notes: Build it if you want a free MRR dashboard, not if you want anyone to believe it. The moat is that the verifier is not you, plus enough listings that readers already know the badge.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted Stripe MRR dashboard with an embeddable SVG badge. Local, single service, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20 with TypeScript, Hono as the HTTP server, run with tsx in dev
- better-sqlite3 for a local snapshots.db file
- stripe official Node SDK
- No frontend framework. One server-rendered HTML page with inline CSS.

Env, read from .env via dotenv, and write a .env.example:
- STRIPE_SECRET_KEY (restricted, read-only on subscriptions, invoices, customers)
- BADGE_LABEL, default "MRR"
- PORT, default 8787

Core logic:
- Fetch all subscriptions with status active or trialing, auto-paginate.
- Normalize each subscription item to a monthly amount: divide yearly by 12, multiply weekly by 52/12, handle quantity and per-unit prices, skip tiered prices and log them as unsupported.
- Sum per currency. Do not convert currencies, report each separately and treat the largest as primary.
- Also compute active subscriber count, MRR added and churned in the last 30 days from subscription created and canceled_at timestamps.
- Cache the result in SQLite as a timestamped snapshot. Refresh at most once per hour; serve cache otherwise.

Routes:
- GET / : HTML page showing primary MRR, subscriber count, 30 day net change, a sparkline built from stored snapshots as inline SVG, and the last refresh time.
- GET /badge.svg : shields-style SVG badge, label from BADGE_LABEL, value like "$4,210/mo", fixed width text measurement is fine, Cache-Control max-age 3600.
- GET /api/mrr : JSON of the latest snapshot.
- POST /refresh : force a refresh, ignore the hourly limit.

Explicitly out of scope: auth, multi-user, other payment providers, cryptographic proof, and any claim of independent verification. Put a comment at the top of badge.ts stating plainly that a self-hosted badge is self-attested and proves nothing to third parties.

Deliver: README with setup, the restricted key scopes needed, a curl example, and a note on deploying behind a reverse proxy. Include one vitest file covering the yearly and weekly interval normalization math.
